subject: Accounting
title: The Factory System's Numbers
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Factory System's Numbers.

hook.text: A factory makes 10,000 widgets. How much does each one cost? In 1900, that was a hard question.

buildup.text: Factories had to allocate rent, labor, materials, and overhead across thousands of products.

discovery.text: Standard costing emerged—predicting what each product should cost, then tracking variances.

twist.text: Managers who understood costs could undercut competitors. Those who didn't went bankrupt.

climax.text: Cost control became a competitive weapon, not just a record-keeping exercise.

punchline.text: Know your costs or lose to someone who does.

quiz.question: What is standard costing?
options: Predicting product costs and tracking differences

details.summary: The factory system of the Industrial Revolution demanded entirely new accounting methods to track raw materials, labor costs, and production output across complex manufacturing operations, giving birth to cost accounting.
details.whyItMatters: Factory accounting created the discipline of cost accounting, which remains essential for any manufacturing or production business trying to understand and control what it costs to make products.
takeaways: Factories needed to track costs of raw materials, labor, and overhead that simple merchant accounting couldn't handle
Cost accounting emerged to help factory owners understand and control production expenses
The factory system drove the separation of financial accounting from management accounting

faq.question: Why did factories need new accounting methods?
faq.answer: Merchant accounting only tracked buying and selling. Factories needed to calculate the cost of raw materials, labor, machine time, and overhead for each product. This complexity required entirely new methods to understand whether production was profitable.

faq.question: What is cost accounting and how did it originate?
faq.answer: Cost accounting is the practice of tracking and analyzing the costs of producing goods. It originated in the Industrial Revolution when factory owners needed to understand exactly what each product cost to make, including materials, labor, and a share of factory overhead.
